text: Roman Gregory Chatov (1900–1987) was a Russian-born American artist, painter, designer, and illustrator. Born in Rostov-on-Don, Russia, to a theater impresario and his wife, Chatov began drawing in his teenage years, creating magazine illustrations at age 16 and serving as a military-correspondent painter near the end of World War I. He received his initial art training in Russia and Paris, France. In 1922, he moved to New York with his family due to the Bolshevik Revolution and the Bolshevik victory in the Russian Civil War. He later joined the Art Students League and the National Academy of Art to further develop his skills. Chatov initially designed costumes and painted murals, including works for the Ford and Palestinian Pavilions at the 1939 New York World's Fair under a commission from the New Deal Works Progress Administration. Among his most notable works was a set of murals for New York City's Russian Tea Room restaurant, which are now held in a New York City museum. These achievements led to numerous painting commissions across the United States. He also designed costumes for Florenz Ziegfeld, and dancer Isadora Duncan admired his designs; he painted a silk scarf for her, which later caused her death when it became entangled in the wheel of a moving car. In New York, Chatov met prominent artists such as Willem de Kooning, with whom he shared studio space. Under commission from MGM, Chatov and his brother Constantin painted portraits of famous Hollywood celebrities, including Vivien Leigh and Clark Gable. Chatov married Geneva McCormack in 1942. In his later years, he focused primarily on portraiture and opened an art studio in Atlanta with his brother Constantin. He received the Governor's Award from the Georgia Council for the Arts and Humanities in 1983 and died in 1987 at the age of 86 or 87. His son Marc Chatov (born in 1953) continues his father's legacy as an artist and art instructor.
